The term flak comes from the German Flugabwehrkanone, meaning 'aircraft defense cannon,' used during World War II to describe German anti-aircraft fire aimed at Allied bombers. English-speaking pilots adopted and shortened the word to refer to the bursting shells that filled the sky around them. By the late 1940s, flak had entered everyday English as a metaphor for harsh criticism — a way of describing the feeling of being 'under fire' without a single shot being fired.
